qs.q: A 9-year-old child with type 1 diabetes mellitus presents with deep, rapid breathing, fruity breath, and confusion. Laboratory findings include pH 7.10, serum bicarbonate 10 mmol/L, and high anion gap. What is the primary biochemical origin of this metabolic acidosis?
o: Hepatic overproduction of acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate acids
Decreased renal excretion of filtered inorganic phosphate complexes
Accumulation of exogenous organic toxins filtered by damaged glomeruli
Massive cellular lysis releasing intracellular organic amino acids
Inhibition of the Krebs cycle by unchecked peripheral insulin activity
qs.e: Absolute insulin deficiency causes unrestrained lipolysis, leading hepatic metabolism to generate large amounts of ketoacids like beta-hydroxybutyrate.
qs.s: Weekly Year 4: Paediatrics Exam - November 13, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: During a routine metabolic investigation, a patient's plasma sample demonstrates a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis accompanied by severe hyperkalemia. Which upstream enzymatic pathway or transport process is primarily impaired?
o: Impaired proximal tubular reabsorption of filtered bicarbonate
Defective hepatic urea cycle conversion of ammonia to urea
Impaired aldosterone-mediated distal nephron potassium secretion
Deficient pancreatic exocrine secretion of alkaline fluid
Impaired erythrocyte carbonic anhydrase catalysis of carbon dioxide
qs.e: Type 4 renal tubular acidosis involves aldosterone deficiency or resistance, impairing distal potassium and hydrogen ion excretion.
qs.s: Weekly Year 2: Clinical Biochemistry Exam - November 13, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A patient with poorly controlled type 1 diabetes presents with deep, rapid breathing and a high anion gap metabolic acidosis. What is the fundamental biochemical driver of this state?
o: Renal failure prevents the excretion of filtered organic acid anions
Unchecked lipolysis floods the liver with precursors for ketone bodies
Severe tissue hypoxia forces cells to rely exclusively on glycolysis
Exogenous acid ingestion overwhelms the body buffering capacity systems
Excessive protein catabolism releases large quantities of sulfuric acid
qs.e: Insulin deficiency activates hormone-sensitive lipase, increasing free fatty acids that the liver converts into acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate.

qs.q: A 50-year-old trauma victim receives three litres of 0.9% normal saline rapidly during initial stabilization for a bleeding liver laceration. Laboratory results subsequently reveal a hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis. Which underlying mechanism explains this electrolyte and acid-base disturbance?
o: Dilutional thrombocytopenia impairs systemic cellular oxygen capacity
Rapid expansion of extracellular fluid dilutes endogenous bicarbonate pools
High supraphysiologic chloride load overwhelms renal tubular excretion
Excessive sodium retention drives secondary intracellular potassium shifts
Crystalloid-induced renal vasoconstriction causes acute tubular retention
qs.e: Normal saline contains high chloride levels which cause non-anion gap metabolic acidosis when infused rapidly.

qs.q: A trauma patient undergoing an emergent damage control laparotomy develops coagulopathy, hypothermia, and persistent metabolic acidosis. The surgical team decides to pack the abdomen and terminate the procedure. Which pathophysiological triad does this timely intervention specifically aim to break?
o: The metabolic triad of hyperglycemia, ketosis, and severe dehydration
The septic triad of bacteremia, vasodilation, and myocardial depression
The lethal triad of acidosis, hypothermia, and consumptive coagulopathy
The obstructive triad of tamponade, tension, and venous return failure
The hypoxic triad of cyanosis, hypercapnia, and pulmonary vasoconstriction
qs.e: Damage control surgery interrupts the lethal triad of hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy.

qs.q: A 40-year-old man with poorly controlled Type 1 diabetes mellitus presents with rapid breathing, confusion, and fruity breath odor. Arterial blood gas shows severe metabolic acidosis. Which compensatory mechanism is primarily responsible for restoring his pH?
o: Renal reabsorption of filtered bicarbonate in tubules.
Hepatic conversion of excess ketoacids into urea.
Kussmaul breathing driving off carbon dioxide via lungs.
Intracellular buffering via rapid potassium shifts.
Enhanced secretion of titratable acids in nephrons.
qs.e: Respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis involves hyperventilation to reduce arterial PCO2.

qs.q: A 3-year-old child presents with lethargy, poor feeding, and deep, rapid breathing. Laboratory results show a blood glucose of 28 mmol/L, serum bicarbonate of 10 mEq/L, and a high anion gap metabolic acidosis. What is the fundamental pathophysiological mechanism driving the tachypnea in this patient?
o: Renal compensation trying to eliminate volatile respiratory acids
Peripherally mediated reflex due to severe systemic dehydration
Direct central nervous system stimulation by circulating ketones
Hypoxemia resulting from secondary aspiration of gastric contents
Respiratory compensation to eliminate excess carbon dioxide
qs.e: Kussmaul breathing is a respiratory compensation mechanism to eliminate carbon dioxide and mitigate severe metabolic acidosis.

qs.q: A 3-year-old child presents with lethargy, poor feeding, and deep Kussmaul breathing. Blood gas analysis reveals severe metabolic acidosis with high anion gap and marked hyperglycemia. What is the immediate physiological trigger for the increased lipolysis seen in this condition?
o: Elevated serum osmolality causing cellular dehydration
Direct toxic effect of excess glucose on adipose
Primary hyperfunction of the adrenal cortex
Peripheral tissue resistance to thyroid hormone
Insulin deficiency coupled with excess counter-hormones
qs.e: Insulin deficiency and high counter-regulatory hormones activate hormone-sensitive lipase, driving excessive lipolysis and ketogenesis.

es.q: Explain how to calculate the anion gap and classify metabolic acidosis based on its anion gap values.
es.m:
- **Formula:** Anion gap = (Na + K) − (Cl + HCO3).
- **Normal values:** 8 to 16 mmol/L (or 3 to 11 mmol/L without potassium).
- **Significance:** Represents unmeasured anions such as albumin, phosphate, sulphate, and organic acids.
- **High anion gap causes:** Lactic acidosis (shock, sepsis, ischaemic bowel), diabetic ketoacidosis, renal failure, poisoning (salicylates, methanol, ethylene glycol), and starvation.
- **Normal anion gap causes:** Diarrhoea, intestinal fistulae and ileostomy, renal tubular acidosis, pancreatic fistula, excess saline (hyperchloraemic acidosis), carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, and ureteric diversion.
es.s: Surgical Critical Care: ICU, Respiratory Failure, Ventilation, Blood: Essay ques

es.q: A patient with a history of Sjögren's syndrome develops a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis with hypokalaemia and persistently alkaline urine (pH > 5.5). This presentation is most characteristic of which type of RTA? → Type 1 (Distal) RTA
es.m: **Diagnosis**,- Most characteristic of Type 1 (Distal) RTA.,- Defect in alpha-intercalated cells of the distal tubule.,- Inability to secrete H+ ions leads to alkaline urine (pH > 5.5).,- Associated with hypokalaemia.,- Common causes include Sjögren's syndrome and autoimmune diseases.,- Results in normal anion gap metabolic acidosis.

exam: A 6‑year‑old with severe watery diarrhoea presents with lethargy – what investigations and immediate management would you prioritize? — ABG, electrolytes, calculate anion gap; give IV isotonic saline with bicarbonate if pH <7.20.

A patient with malaria develops metabolic acidosis; how does the anion gap help you, and what specific therapy is added? — High anion gap suggests lactate; start aggressive fluid resuscitation, treat malaria, consider bicarbonate only if pH <7.10.

You receive an ABG: pH 7.28, PaCO2 30 mmHg, HCO3 15 mmol/L. What is the primary disorder and is compensation appropriate? — Primary metabolic acidosis; expected PaCO2 ≈ 1.5×15+8=30 mmHg, so compensation is appropriate.

A diabetic patient arrives in ketoacidosis with pH 7.15. Which drug class is essential and why must you avoid which alternative? — Insulin is essential to stop ketogenesis; avoid sulfonylureas because they can worsen hypoglycaemia once glucose falls.

In a resource‑limited clinic, lactate measurement is unavailable. How would you suspect lactic acidosis clinically? — Look for shock, mottled skin, rapid breathing, and high anion gap with normal chloride.

A patient on chronic kidney disease presents with pH 7.32, HCO3 18 mmol/L, and PaCO2 30 mmHg. What is the likely chronicity and next step? — Chronic metabolic acidosis with partial respiratory compensation; arrange dialysis planning and dietary bicarbonate.
How does a mixed high‑anion‑gap and normal‑gap acidosis appear on delta‑gap analysis? — ΔAG > ΔHCO3 by >6 mmol/L, indicating an additional normal‑gap component.
Why is sodium bicarbonate contraindicated in severe hyperchloremic acidosis? — It can worsen hyperchloremia and cause volume overload without correcting the underlying chloride excess.

ai.summary: Metabolic acidosis is a primary reduction in plasma bicarbonate causing a low pH. It is common in low‑resource settings from diarrhoea, renal disease, sepsis, and toxic ingestions.

b: Classified by anion gap (high vs. normal)
Acute vs. chronic based on duration and compensation
sections.p: Metabolic acidosis occurs when the body loses bicarbonate or gains acid faster than compensatory mechanisms can correct, resulting in arterial pH <7.35.

b: Calculate anion gap: Na – (Cl + HCO3); normal 8‑12 mmol/L
sections.p: Identify the type, severity, and underlying cause to guide urgent management.

b: Uncorrected severe acidosis (<7.20) can cause vasodilation, arrhythmias, and decreased myocardial contractility
Rapid correction of chronic acidosis may precipitate hypokalemia
sections.p: In East African hospitals, the most frequent precipitants are diarrhoeal loss of bicarbonate, renal failure, severe malaria, sepsis, and toxic ingestions (e.g., methanol, ethylene glycol).
